title: Studying Abroad at the University of Adelaide
paragraphs: I studied abroad at the University of Adelaide in Australia from the end of March to mid-June.

Adelaide is a cozy city, and I think it is quite safe even compared with other cities in Australia. Beaches and wineries spread out nearby, and in the city center there are wide roads and beautiful rows of broadleaf trees, so it is a very beautiful and livable place. In fact, it is ranked fifth in the world's most livable cities ranking. For traveling around Australia the transport (air access) is somewhat inconvenient, but even taking that off, it is a very good place.

During these three months I rotated through psychiatry, pediatrics and emergency medicine, doing a clerkship in each for one month. I would like to explain what the clerkships were like. Incidentally, in Australia paper charts were basically used.

In psychiatry, I mainly took part on the ward in meetings with patients, families and social workers, and filled in charts and minutes. I also gave presentations on rounds and was allowed to write discharge summaries. Unlike Japan, in Australian psychiatry there is a great deal of intervention by social workers and meetings were held frequently, so I could write many charts and records every day. In psychiatry, each student is assigned one fixed supervising doctor and acts together with that doctor for the whole month, so you become quite close to the doctor and can be taught thoroughly. I also visited a nearby community center and the emergency department, and was allowed to see how general practitioners deal with mental illness and how patients suspected of mental illness brought to the emergency department are triaged.

In pediatrics the fields are subdivided, and I did clerkships in pediatric gastroenterology, pediatric neurology and pediatric respiratory medicine. I went on rounds with the doctors, was allowed to fill in charts and do physical examinations, and had the doctors explain things in the outpatient clinic. There were many interesting differences from Japan, such as diseases rarely seen in Japan (cystic fibrosis and coeliac disease) being commonly seen in Australia. I was also able to attend lectures with local students. Although the lectures were in English, they were very easy to understand and very instructive.

In emergency medicine, I basically took histories from several patients every day and consulted the senior doctor. After consulting, I saw the patient again together with the doctor, but after that it was basically left to the students, so, while asking the doctors various things, I did blood draws, IVs, suturing, and writing letters to the general practitioner (something like a discharge summary). As for the letters (summaries), at first the result was terrible, with the doctor rewriting everything, but as I wrote several of them, the number of corrected places decreased, and in the second half I became able to hand them to patients without anything being corrected. I was very happy to feel my own growth. Also, several patients categorized as "mental illness" came every day without fail, so I actively took histories from such patients as well. Since in Japan I had little chance to see patients with drug intoxication or mental illness, it was very interesting.

Another thing I felt throughout the clerkships is that everyone working in the hospital was very cheerful and seemed to enjoy working. There were people of various professions in the hospital, senior doctors, intern doctors, nurses and social workers, but they all addressed each other by first name, and a relationship of trust in which they could say anything to each other was firmly built. The atmosphere was very comfortable, and I felt it was perhaps typical of Australia.

By studying abroad this time, I think my reluctance to speak to people on my own initiative and to ask questions has decreased considerably. In particular, the emergency medicine clerkship began each morning with introducing myself to a different doctor, and I also had to talk to patients I was seeing for the first time, so it became practice in speaking on my own to people I did not know. Furthermore, the doctors were all very kind and taught me thoroughly whatever I asked, so I naturally came to ask many questions. At the same time, I came to listen to the doctors while thinking so that I could always ask something, and I think it was very good that I acquired this attitude. I also traveled to various places in the country, and I was able to spend my free time very meaningfully, touching magnificent nature that one cannot see in Japan and dealing on my own with happenings that one would never experience in Japan.

The people I met in Australia were all very friendly and kind, and always smiled at me. This was not because I was liked; basically everyone in this country treats everybody with a smile. When I did clerkships and lived in Japan, I had never been smiled at and called by name this much. I had not thought that being called by name and treated with a smile would be this happy. I came to like Australia, with its many kind and warm people, very much, and I sincerely think it was good that I studied abroad.

Finally, I would like to thank everyone in the International Collaboration Office and the Frontier Association for creating the opportunity to study abroad. And above all, to the two who spent the three months with me, thanks to you I was able to have a very enjoyable three months. Thank you very much.
